To: Engineering leadership
From: Platform/AI working group
Re: Buy more local AI hardware or improve utilisation of what we own

Recommendation up front: do not approve a broad hardware purchase yet. Fund a short utilisation and reliability program first, then buy only the capacity that survives evidence. If the program shows a durable interactive bottleneck, add targeted local capacity or a bounded cloud burst; if it shows mostly idle GPUs and bursty batch work, keep the hardware and change scheduling.

The tempting case for more hardware is simple: demand is rising, queues are growing, and waiting feels risky. But the current numbers do not yet prove that the constraint is silicon rather than scheduling, model choice, or workload design. Local hardware is expensive to own and slow to change. It carries power, cooling, rack space, maintenance, spare parts, staffing, and depreciation. It also creates a temptation to keep models resident that are rarely used, which lowers effective capacity and increases tail latency. Buying more machines before we understand the shape of demand risks repeating the same mistake with a larger bill.

Cost should be evaluated as total cost per useful inference, not per GPU. A machine that is idle 70 percent of the time is not cheap; it is a fixed cost with poor marginal value. Conversely, a modest increase in utilisation can be worth more than a new node. We should track tokens per second, requests per second, p50 and p95 latency, queue depth, GPU memory pressure, batch fill rate, model load time, and the fraction of time each accelerator is doing useful work rather than waiting, swapping, or serving stale models. We should also separate interactive product traffic from offline batch jobs. Interactive traffic needs low latency and predictable capacity; batch traffic can tolerate queueing and can often be moved to cheaper or more elastic capacity.

Latency is where the decision becomes concrete. If p95 latency is dominated by queueing behind batch jobs, the fix is isolation and scheduling, not more GPUs. If p95 is dominated by model size and memory pressure, the fix may be quantization, smaller distilled models, better caching, or a different serving stack. If latency is already acceptable but throughput is capped, then capacity may be justified. Reliability matters just as much. More hardware increases the number of components, but it can also improve resilience if it is used to create failure domains, redundancy, and cleaner rollouts. The risk is that a small team will add nodes without adding observability, runbooks, or capacity headroom, turning a performance problem into an operational one.

Opportunity cost is easy to miss. Every week spent tuning utilisation is a week not spent on product features, but the alternative is not free either. A large purchase consumes capital, slows iteration, and can lock us into a hardware generation that becomes obsolete as models and serving stacks evolve. Local ownership also competes with cloud burst capacity, which is less efficient at steady state but more reversible. The right question is not “local or cloud” but “which workloads deserve fixed local capacity, and which should remain elastic.”

Reversibility should be a first-class criterion. Leases, reserved instances, modular racks, and cloud burst are easier to unwind than a large purchase. A purchase is justified when the workload is stable, latency-sensitive, and expected to persist beyond the hardware’s useful life. It is weaker when demand is uncertain, models are changing quickly, or the workload is mostly batch and can be scheduled around cheaper capacity.

I acknowledge uncertainty. Forecasts are noisy, model demand may shift, and pricing can move. I do not have enough confidence to commit to a fixed number of GPUs today. What I do have is enough confidence to reject a blanket purchase.

Proposed path: for the next six to eight weeks, instrument the serving layer, separate interactive from batch traffic, enforce per-team quotas, cache aggressively, and retire unused models. Review weekly. If interactive p95 remains above target after scheduling and model changes, approve a targeted purchase or a bounded burst plan. If utilisation rises and latency improves, defer the purchase and revisit with a quarterly capacity review. This is not the fastest route to more hardware, but it is the most reversible, and it gives us evidence before we commit.
